title: Rereading chapters 21–24
tomorrow: what makes someone worthy: their family, or something else?

cards: A post goes up at nine. By a quarter past, the app has been opened eleven times. The likes are coming slower than last time, so the thumb keeps going back, and every check makes the next one more likely, not less.
The Dhammapada's chapter on thirst has a picture for exactly this. It's a plant: a creeper, the kind of vine that climbs the fence and then the tree and then the roof.

teach.b: In Max Müller's translation: “The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest.”

Thirst is the book's word for craving, tanha in Pali: not wanting a glass of water, but the restless wanting that never quite drinks its fill. Two pictures in one verse. The creeper grows by being fed.

teach.h: THE MONKEY GRABS THE NEXT BRANCH.
teach.b: The monkey grabs one branch, then the next, and never stays in the tree it's in. Reread now, the chapters around it read like a week's worth of help for that monkey.
The elephant chapter gives a way to stand still under a hard comment: “Silently shall I endure abuse as the elephant in battle endures the arrow sent from the bow: for the world is ill-natured.”

The miscellaneous chapter offers a trade: leave a small pleasure if you can see a greater one. The chapter on thirst closes the loop with its own scale: the extinction of thirst, it says, overcomes all pain.

teach.h: THE VINE SLOWS WHEN IT ISN'T FED.
teach.b: The near end is smaller and more honest: the vine slows when it isn't fed. One check skipped. One comparison not made.
Nobody becomes thirstless in an afternoon.
But less thirsty is something a person can notice by evening.

how: Buddhist teachers speak of tanha, craving, as the root of suffering in the Buddha's second noble truth; in meditation, some practice noticing a craving arise and pass without acting on it.

games.q: four chapters for a thirsty week — tap the pairs.
p: thirst that grows as it's fed
worth leaving for a greater one

s: in the Dhammapada, thirst means needing a drink of water
it's craving, tanha: the restless wanting that never drinks its fill.
the elephant verse says to strike back at abuse
it says to endure abuse silently, as the elephant in battle endures the arrow.
the Dhammapada says the thirst of a thoughtless person grows like a creeper
verse 334: it grows like a creeper, and the person runs like a monkey seeking fruit.

games.q: your cousin got a new phone a month ago and is already counting down to the next one. what does the thirst chapter say is going on?
o: the creeper: the wanting grows as it's fed; the next phone won't end it.
he just picked the wrong phone; the right one would finally satisfy him.
he's doing it wrong by owning a phone at all; wanting nothing is the goal.
games.why: the verse puts the trouble in the thirst, not the phone. the monkey always sees fruit on the next branch.

practice: If there's water nearby, take one slow sip and hold it in your mouth a moment before swallowing. Notice where the thirst eases, and how quickly it's forgotten.
Then, for the rest of the sit, watch for the next small want, the urge to check something, and let it pass without feeding it.

wordCard.voice: Rereading chapters 21 to 24: the miscellaneous, the downward course, the elephant and thirst, read again. At the center, the creeper: craving grows as it's fed.

orig.note: Pali: thirst, craving (Sanskrit tṛṣṇā); the twenty-fourth chapter is the Taṇhāvagga, the chapter on thirst.

carryVoice: One line for today: less thirsty, not thirstless, and that's enough to notice. Six of seven down.
